reference_text:
Welcome to the course. We will work through each concept carefully, connect the
ideas step by step, and use practical examples to make technical topics easier
to understand. When we introduce a new method, focus first on the problem it
solves and why it is useful. For example, in machine learning, features are the
information we give the model, while the target is what we want it to predict.
Now consider a simple question: what changes when the data contains missing
values? We will think through the reason and then look at the code. In Python,
we can inspect the data, run one small step at a time, and explain what the
result means. The goal is to understand the logic, not simply memorize syntax.

slides.title: Big picture
slides.transcript:
Welcome to Module 6, Joining Data in PostgreSQL. Up to this point, many of our examples have focused on one table at a time. That is useful for learning SQL, but real analytical work usually requires information that is stored across several related tables. A healthcare system may store patients in one table, admissions in another, lab results in another, and staff information somewhere else. A university may separate students, registrations, courses, and grades. An online store may separate customers, orders, products, and payments.

[tts-break]

In this module, the important skill is not simply memorizing JOIN syntax. I want you to think about what the final rows mean. If one patient has several admissions, should that patient appear once or several times? If a patient has no admission, should that patient disappear, or should the patient remain with missing admission values? Those questions determine how we join the data.

[tts-break]

As we work through the module, keep four questions in mind. First, what should one output row represent? Second, which rows must be preserved even when no match exists? Third, what rule tells us that two rows belong together? And fourth, after the join runs, how can we validate that the result makes sense? If you build the habit of answering those four questions, JOINs become much easier to reason about.

slides.title: Learning objectives
slides.transcript:
By the end of this module, you should be able to choose a join based on the business question rather than simply choosing the join type you remember first. For example, the phrase only patients who have admissions suggests a different join from every patient, whether or not an admission exists.

[tts-break]

You will also practice using aliases, ON conditions, and USING. Aliases are especially important when several tables contain columns with similar names. They help us state clearly which table a column comes from and make longer SQL queries easier to read.

[tts-break]

A major goal is understanding grain and cardinality. Grain means what one row represents. One row could represent one patient, one admission, one lab test, or one department. Cardinality describes how many rows on one side can match rows on the other side. One patient may match several admissions, and several one-to-many relationships can cause row multiplication if we are not careful.

[tts-break]

Finally, you should be able to validate a joined dataset. We will compare row counts, count distinct keys, inspect known examples, and check unmatched cases. A query that runs without an error is not automatically a correct analytical result.

slides.title: Join decision workflow
slides.transcript:
Here is the workflow I want you to use whenever you build a join. Start by defining the grain. Before writing SQL, say in plain language what one row in the final result should represent. Maybe the target is one patient, one admission, one student registration, or one sales transaction.

[tts-break]

Next, identify the row sets you are combining. Then define the matching rule. Usually the relationship uses a key such as patient ID, customer ID, or course ID. Do not assume that columns should be joined just because they have similar names. The relationship should make sense in the data model.

[tts-break]

After that, decide which unmatched rows must remain. If the requirement says every patient, then the patient population must be preserved. If the requirement says only patients with admissions, then a match is required.

[tts-break]

Then predict cardinality. Ask whether each row can match zero rows, one row, or many rows on the other side. Finally, validate the output. Compare your predicted result with the actual row count and inspect a few known cases. The core habit is simple: start from the business rule, not from a JOIN keyword.

slides.title: Practice schema
slides.transcript:
The practice database for this module is a small synthetic healthcare database. The patients table contains one row per patient. Admissions, lab results, and prescriptions are child tables, which means a single patient can have several related rows in each of those tables.

[tts-break]

We also have medical staff and departments. Staff members belong to departments, and admissions can reference an attending staff member. These relationships let us practice both simple joins and multi-table join paths.

[tts-break]

The database intentionally contains useful edge cases. There is a patient with no admission activity, a department with no activity, and a staging record whose patient ID does not appear in the official patient master. Those cases help us see the difference between INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, and FULL OUTER joins.

[tts-break]

As you work through the examples, remember that repeated values are not automatically errors. If one patient has two admissions, the patient information may legitimately appear twice in an admission-level result. The key question is always what one output row represents.

slides.title: Join mental model
slides.transcript:
A useful way to think about a join is to separate three ideas: row sets, matching, and preservation.

[tts-break]

First, identify the two row sets being compared. For example, we may compare patients with admissions. Second, define what makes two rows related. In our healthcare example, an admission matches a patient when the patient IDs are equal. That matching rule belongs in the ON condition.

[tts-break]

Third, decide what happens when a row has no match. That is the preservation question. INNER JOIN does not preserve unmatched rows. LEFT JOIN preserves unmatched rows from the left side. RIGHT JOIN preserves unmatched rows from the right side. FULL OUTER JOIN preserves unmatched rows from both sides.

[tts-break]

This distinction is important because the ON condition and the JOIN type have different jobs. ON controls matching. The JOIN type controls which unmatched rows survive. Before you run a join, try to describe it in one sentence: compare these two row sets, match them using this rule, and preserve these unmatched rows.

slides.title: Row preservation map
slides.transcript:
Before we use the larger practice database, this slide gives us a very small example that we can reuse to understand all four major join types.

[tts-break]

On the left, the patients table has Ana with ID 1, Ben with ID 2, and Cara with ID 3. On the right, the admissions table contains two admissions for patient 1, one admission for patient 3, and one admission for patient 4. Patient 4 does not exist in our tiny patient table. This small mismatch is intentional because it lets us see what each join preserves.

[tts-break]

With an INNER JOIN, we keep only matching combinations. Ben disappears because patient 2 has no admission, and admission 104 disappears because patient 4 has no patient row. With a LEFT JOIN, every patient remains, so Ben stays and the admission columns for Ben become NULL. With a RIGHT JOIN, every admission remains, so admission 104 stays and its patient columns become NULL. With a FULL OUTER JOIN, both unmatched cases remain.

[tts-break]

Use this as your prediction habit. Before you run the SQL, ask which unmatched rows should survive and where NULL values should appear.

slides.title: INNER JOIN
slides.transcript:
Now let us focus on INNER JOIN. Look first at the small tables at the top of the slide. Ana has two matching admissions, Ben has no matching admission, and Cara has one matching admission. Admission 104 belongs to patient ID 4, which does not exist in the small patient table.

[tts-break]

The INNER JOIN result contains only matching combinations. Ana appears twice because she has two admissions. Cara appears once. Ben disappears because there is no matching admission, and admission 104 disappears because there is no matching patient. This is the main idea of INNER JOIN: both sides must participate in a match.

[tts-break]

Now look at the runnable PostgreSQL query. We give patients the alias p and admissions the alias a. The ON condition says that an admission matches a patient when their patient IDs are equal. The selected columns combine information from both tables.

[tts-break]

In the current Module 6 practice database, there are twelve admission records, and every admission references a valid patient. Therefore this INNER JOIN returns exactly twelve rows. That does not mean there are twelve different patients. Some patients have more than one admission. The grain is one matching admission with patient information attached.

[tts-break]

When you run the query, do not only ask whether it executes. Compare the result with your prediction. Check repeated patient IDs and confirm that each repeated row represents a different admission.

slides.title: Aliases and grain
slides.transcript:
Aliases and grain solve two different kinds of confusion.

[tts-break]

Aliases make the SQL easier to read. If both patients and admissions contain a patient ID column, writing p dot patient ID and a dot patient ID makes the source explicit. As queries grow to three, four, or five tables, this becomes very important. Once you assign an alias to a table, use that alias consistently.

[tts-break]

Grain helps us interpret the result. Suppose a patient has two admissions. After joining patients to admissions, the patient name may appear twice. That does not automatically mean the data was duplicated incorrectly. If one result row represents one admission, then repeating the patient information is expected.

[tts-break]

A common beginner mistake is seeing repeated values and immediately adding DISTINCT. That can hide a real modeling problem or remove valid events. Before using DISTINCT, ask what each row represents and whether those rows correspond to different real events.

[tts-break]

A good habit is to write a short grain sentence before a complicated query. For this example, the sentence is: one output row represents one admission with patient information attached.

slides.title: LEFT JOIN
slides.transcript:
LEFT JOIN is one of the most useful join patterns in analytics because it lets us preserve a complete population.

[tts-break]

Look at the small tables. Ana has two admissions, Cara has one, and Ben has none. With a LEFT JOIN, the left table is patients, so every patient must remain. Ana appears twice because she has two matching admissions. Cara appears once. Ben also remains, but the admission column is NULL because no admission matched.

[tts-break]

Now connect that visual to the PostgreSQL query. Patients appears before LEFT JOIN, so patients is the preserved side. Admissions is optional. The ON condition still controls matching by patient ID.

[tts-break]

This pattern is common in real projects. A university may want every enrolled student and an advising appointment when one exists. A business may want every customer and the customer's most recent order when available. A hospital may want every patient and a follow-up visit when available. If we used INNER JOIN in those situations, the people with no related activity would disappear.

[tts-break]

Run the query and find the patient with NULL admission values. That NULL is meaningful information. It tells us that the patient was preserved even though no related admission was found.

slides.title: Anti-join
slides.transcript:
An anti-join answers a very practical question: which rows on one side have no related row on the other side?

[tts-break]

The small example shows three patients and only two patients with lab results. We first use a LEFT JOIN because we want to preserve every patient. After that join, the patient with no lab result has NULL values on the lab side. Then we use WHERE and check whether the lab test ID is NULL. That leaves only the patient with no matching lab row.

[tts-break]

The choice of column for the NULL check matters. We should test a right-side key that cannot be NULL for a real matched row. A primary key such as test ID is a good choice. If we test a column that can legitimately contain NULL, we could mistakenly classify a matched record as unmatched.

[tts-break]

This pattern is useful far beyond healthcare. We can find customers with no orders, students with no submission, products with no sales, employees with no required training, or patients with no follow-up activity.

[tts-break]

Read the logic as a sentence: preserve all patients, try to match lab results, then keep only the patients for whom no lab result was found.

slides.title: RIGHT JOIN
slides.transcript:
RIGHT JOIN is the mirror image of LEFT JOIN. Instead of preserving every row from the left side, it preserves every row from the right side.

[tts-break]

In the tiny example, the admissions table is on the right. Admission 104 belongs to patient ID 4, which has no matching patient row. Because the right side is preserved, admission 104 remains in the result and the patient columns become NULL.

[tts-break]

The runnable example uses a different real-world relationship. We join medical staff to departments and preserve every department. If a department has no staff member, the department still appears and the staff columns become NULL.

[tts-break]

RIGHT JOIN is valid PostgreSQL syntax, but many teams prefer to rewrite it as a LEFT JOIN by swapping the table order. That often makes the preserved population easier to see because the table you want to keep appears first.

[tts-break]

So the important lesson is not that RIGHT JOIN is bad. The lesson is to make preservation obvious. If your question says every department, structure the query so another reader can quickly see that departments are the population being preserved.

slides.title: FULL OUTER JOIN
slides.transcript:
FULL OUTER JOIN preserves unmatched rows from both sides. It is especially useful when we are comparing two systems and want to see matches as well as differences.

[tts-break]

Look at the tiny tables. Ben has no admission, so the FULL OUTER result keeps Ben and fills the admission value with NULL. Admission 104 has no matching patient, so that admission also remains and the patient name becomes NULL. Matched rows remain as usual.

[tts-break]

The PostgreSQL example uses a patient master table and an admissions staging table. This is a common data-quality situation. The patient master represents the official source, while the staging table represents imported data. We want to see records that match, patient records with no staging row, and staging rows whose patient ID does not exist in the master.

[tts-break]

The CASE expression translates those situations into readable labels. COALESCE helps us show one identifier even when the row exists on only one side.

[tts-break]

Think of FULL OUTER JOIN as a reconciliation tool. Finance teams use similar logic to compare transaction systems. Human resources teams may compare employee and payroll records. Data engineers use it to compare source and target tables during migrations.

slides.title: Outer join comparison
slides.transcript:
This slide turns the join types into business-language decisions.

[tts-break]

If the question is only about patients who have admissions, then a match is required, so INNER JOIN is appropriate. If the question says every patient, with admission information when available, then the patient population must be preserved, which points to LEFT JOIN when patients is on the left.

[tts-break]

If the question says every department and staff when available, we can preserve departments with RIGHT JOIN if departments is on the right, or we can reorder the tables and use LEFT JOIN. The result can be logically equivalent, but the reordered LEFT JOIN is often easier to read.

[tts-break]

If the goal is to compare two systems and show unmatched records from either side, FULL OUTER JOIN is a natural choice.

[tts-break]

Pay attention to words such as only matched, every, including those with none, and unmatched from either source. Those phrases tell you more about the correct join than memorizing a diagram.

slides.title: ON vs WHERE
slides.transcript:
This slide covers one of the most important ideas in the module. In an outer join, placing a condition in ON can produce a very different population from placing the same condition in WHERE.

[tts-break]

Look at the example on the left. We want every patient, but among lab records we only want Glucose tests to match. The Glucose condition is inside ON. Ana has a Glucose test, so that test matches. Ben and Cara do not have a matching Glucose row, but they remain because the LEFT JOIN still preserves every patient. Their lab values become NULL.

[tts-break]

Now look at the example on the right. The LEFT JOIN happens first, and then WHERE requires the lab test to equal Glucose. Ben and Cara have either a non-Glucose value or a NULL lab value, so those rows fail the final filter. Only Ana remains.

[tts-break]

The rule is simple but powerful. ON controls which rows are eligible to match. WHERE filters the result after the join has produced matched and unmatched rows.

[tts-break]

Whenever an outer join must preserve a full population, be very careful with conditions on the optional side. Ask whether the condition belongs to matching or to final filtering.

slides.title: Filter in ON
slides.transcript:
This slide applies the ON-versus-WHERE rule to a runnable PostgreSQL example.

[tts-break]

The tiny input shows three patients. Ana has both a Glucose and a Cholesterol result. Ben has only Cholesterol. Cara has no lab result. Our business question is not show patients who have Glucose tests. The question is show every patient, and attach a Glucose result when one exists.

[tts-break]

That wording tells us that every patient must remain. The Glucose condition belongs inside ON because it defines which lab rows are allowed to match. Ana gets her Glucose result. Ben remains but gets NULL lab values because his Cholesterol row is not eligible to match. Cara also remains with NULL lab values because there is no lab row at all.

[tts-break]

Run the query and verify that the full patient population remains. This is a very useful pattern for reporting. You may want every product with sales from a specific month, every student with a tutoring visit from a specific semester, or every employee with a required certification when one exists.

[tts-break]

The mental sentence is: preserve every patient, and among lab records allow only Glucose rows to match.

slides.title: WHERE trap
slides.transcript:
Now we move the same Glucose condition from ON into WHERE.

[tts-break]

The LEFT JOIN first creates a result containing Ana's lab rows, Ben's Cholesterol row, and Cara with NULL lab values. At that moment, the left join has preserved every patient.

[tts-break]

Then the WHERE condition runs and keeps only rows whose test name equals Glucose. Ana's Glucose row survives. Ana's Cholesterol row is removed. Ben's Cholesterol row is removed. Cara's NULL value does not equal Glucose, so Cara is also removed.

[tts-break]

This is why a LEFT JOIN can behave like a matched-only result when a right-side condition is placed in WHERE. The JOIN keyword did not change, but the final population did.

[tts-break]

Run this query and compare the result with the previous slide. The difference is not cosmetic. It changes the meaning of the analysis. If the requirement says every patient must remain, this WHERE version is not equivalent to the previous ON version.

slides.title: USING
slides.transcript:
USING is a shorter way to express an equality join when both tables use the same column name for the relationship.

[tts-break]

In this example, both patients and admissions contain a column named patient ID. Instead of writing an ON condition that compares the two columns explicitly, PostgreSQL lets us write USING patient ID.

[tts-break]

The relationship is the same. We are still matching patients and admissions when the patient IDs are equal. One convenience is that the join key appears once in the result rather than as two separate copies.

[tts-break]

USING is helpful when the shared key name is clear and the relationship is a simple equality. It is not appropriate when the two tables use different column names, when multiple conditions are needed, or when the relationship is more complex.

[tts-break]

Whether you write ON or USING, you should still be able to explain the relationship in plain language. Shorter syntax should not replace understanding.

slides.title: SELF JOIN
slides.transcript:
A self join means joining a table to itself. We use two aliases so the same physical table can play two logical roles.

[tts-break]

Look at the small staff table. Ana and Ben are both in department A, while Cara is in department B. We treat one copy of the table as s1 and another copy as s2. Then we match rows when the department is the same.

[tts-break]

If we stopped there, we would get unwanted pairs such as Ana paired with herself, Ben paired with himself, and the same colleague pair in both directions. The condition that the first staff ID must be less than the second staff ID solves both problems. It prevents self-pairs and keeps only one direction for each pair.

[tts-break]

In the result, department A produces one unique colleague pair: Ana and Ben.

[tts-break]

Self joins are useful whenever rows in one table must be compared with other rows from that same table. Examples include employee-manager relationships, comparing earlier and later events, matching products in the same category, or identifying pairs of staff members who share a department.

slides.title: Readmissions self join
slides.transcript:
This self-join example compares admissions with other admissions for the same patient.

[tts-break]

We give the admissions table two aliases. The first alias represents an earlier admission, and the second alias represents a later admission. The patient IDs must match so both admissions belong to the same patient.

[tts-break]

We also require the first admission ID to be less than the second admission ID. That gives the two copies different roles and helps avoid comparing the same pair in both directions.

[tts-break]

Then we calculate the number of days between the earlier discharge date and the later admission date. The WHERE clause keeps cases where that gap is between one and ninety days.

[tts-break]

This is a teaching example of how self joins can compare events within the same entity. Similar logic can compare repeat purchases by one customer, repeated service calls for one machine, or multiple registrations for one student.

[tts-break]

When you run the query, remember the grain. One row now represents a pair of admissions for the same patient, not one individual admission.

slides.title: CROSS JOIN
slides.transcript:
CROSS JOIN creates every possible combination between two row sets.

[tts-break]

The visual example uses two departments and three appointment slots. Two times three gives six combinations. Cardiology is paired with all three time slots, and Internal Medicine is also paired with all three time slots.

[tts-break]

Unlike INNER or LEFT JOIN, CROSS JOIN does not use an ON condition to decide which rows match. Every row on the left combines with every row on the right.

[tts-break]

The PostgreSQL example intentionally limits the department list to two departments so the result stays small and easy to inspect. The appointment slots table has three rows, so the output contains six department-and-time combinations.

[tts-break]

CROSS JOIN can be useful for generating schedules, scenario grids, complete date-product combinations, or test cases. But it can also create extremely large results. Before using it, calculate the expected size as the number of left rows multiplied by the number of right rows.

slides.title: Cross join growth
slides.transcript:
This slide shows why we should estimate the size of a cross join before running it.

[tts-break]

Two rows crossed with three rows produce six combinations. One hundred crossed with one hundred produces ten thousand combinations. Ten thousand crossed with ten thousand produces one hundred million combinations.

[tts-break]

The formula is simply N times M, where N is the number of rows on the left and M is the number of rows on the right. The calculation is easy, but the growth can become very large very quickly.

[tts-break]

CROSS JOIN is not inherently bad. It is useful when every combination is intentional. For example, you might generate every store and every month, every product and every region, or every department and every appointment slot.

[tts-break]

The danger appears when a normal join condition is accidentally omitted. If you expected a few thousand rows and suddenly get millions, one of the first things to check is whether a relationship condition is missing and the query has effectively created a Cartesian product.

slides.title: Cardinality
slides.transcript:
Cardinality describes how many rows can match across a relationship.

[tts-break]

In a one-to-one relationship, each key matches at most one row on each side. In a one-to-many relationship, one parent row can match several child rows. A patient-to-admissions relationship is one-to-many because one patient can have several admissions.

[tts-break]

The larger risk appears when several one-to-many child tables are joined independently to the same parent. Suppose one patient has two admissions, two lab results, and two prescriptions. If we join all three detail tables directly by patient ID, the database can produce two times two times two, or eight, combinations.

[tts-break]

Those eight rows do not represent eight new medical events. They represent combinations of existing events. This is a common source of inflated counts in analytical SQL.

[tts-break]

Before joining, estimate whether each relationship is zero-to-one, one-to-one, or one-to-many. That prediction helps you recognize when the output row count is reasonable and when multiplication is occurring.

slides.title: Row multiplication
slides.transcript:
This slide makes row multiplication concrete using Alice in the practice data.

[tts-break]

Alice has two admissions, two lab tests, and two prescriptions. These are six real source records across three child tables. But if we join all three child tables independently by patient ID, each admission can combine with each lab result and each prescription.

[tts-break]

Two admissions times two labs times two prescriptions produces eight joined combinations. The table on the slide shows the eight possible admission-lab-prescription combinations.

[tts-break]

The SQL underneath measures this effect. COUNT star tells us how many joined combinations exist. COUNT DISTINCT admission ID tells us how many unique admissions exist. The same idea is used for lab test IDs and prescription IDs.

[tts-break]

Run the query and compare joined rows with the distinct event counts. This is an important debugging technique. If joined rows are much larger than the number of real events, the query may be combining several one-to-many relationships.

[tts-break]

The rows are not necessarily duplicate rows in the technical sense. They may be unique combinations. The analytical problem is that those combinations can inflate measures if we count them as if each row were a new event.

slides.title: COUNT trap
slides.transcript:
COUNT star answers a very specific question: how many rows are in the current result?

[tts-break]

After a multi-table join, that may not be the same question as how many admissions exist, how many lab tests exist, or how many prescriptions exist. In our example, the raw join creates eight row combinations even though Alice has only two admissions, two labs, and two prescriptions.

[tts-break]

This is why COUNT star can be misleading after joins. It counts the combinations produced by the join.

[tts-break]

One safer approach is to count a distinct event identifier, such as COUNT DISTINCT admission ID. Another approach is to summarize each child table to the target grain before joining. Which approach is better depends on the analytical question.

[tts-break]

Do not add DISTINCT automatically whenever a count looks too large. First define the event you are trying to count. Then choose a method that counts that event correctly.

slides.title: Pre-aggregate first
slides.transcript:
Pre-aggregation is one of the clearest ways to protect a higher-level grain.

[tts-break]

Instead of joining raw admissions, raw lab results, and raw prescriptions to patients, we first summarize each child table by patient ID. The admission summary produces at most one row per patient. The lab summary produces at most one row per patient. The prescription summary does the same.

[tts-break]

Now the three child sources are already at patient grain. When we join those summaries to the patients table, the two-times-two-times-two explosion cannot occur.

[tts-break]

The query uses common table expressions to create the three summaries. Then it LEFT JOINs each summary to patients so patients with no activity are still preserved. COALESCE converts missing counts from NULL to zero.

[tts-break]

This pattern is common in dashboards and feature tables. A customer-level dashboard might summarize orders, support tickets, and refunds separately before combining them. A student-level dataset might summarize registrations, submissions, and advising visits separately.

[tts-break]

The key idea is to make each source compatible with the target grain before combining the sources.

slides.title: Validation checklist
slides.transcript:
A join is not finished when the SQL runs. We still need to validate the result.

[tts-break]

Start with counts. Compare the number of rows before and after the join. If the target should contain one row per patient, compare COUNT star with COUNT DISTINCT patient ID. If those numbers are very different, investigate why.

[tts-break]

Next, inspect keys. Check whether primary keys repeat and whether that repetition is expected at the chosen grain. A patient ID repeating in an admission-level result may be correct. An admission ID repeating in a result that should contain one row per admission may indicate a problem.

[tts-break]

Then spot-check known examples. Choose one entity with multiple related records and one entity with no related records. Those cases often reveal preservation and cardinality problems quickly.

[tts-break]

Finally, write a grain sentence. For example: one row represents one patient with summarized activity counts. If you cannot clearly describe what one row means, the query may still be logically unclear even if the syntax is correct.

slides.title: Multiple joins
slides.transcript:
Real analytical queries often follow a relationship path across more than two tables.

[tts-break]

In this example, we begin with patients and join to admissions using patient ID. Then we join admissions to medical staff using the attending staff ID. The final row contains patient information, admission information, and information about the attending clinician.

[tts-break]

Notice that the second join uses a different key from the first join. We are not connecting tables just because they contain a similar column. We are following the documented relationship path: patient to admission, then admission to attending staff.

[tts-break]

The staff join is a LEFT JOIN because we may want to keep the admission even if the staff reference is missing. If each attending staff ID points to at most one staff member, adding the staff table should not increase the number of admission rows.

[tts-break]

This same design appears in other domains. Retail might follow customer to order to payment. Education might follow student to registration to course. Writing the relationship path before writing the SQL makes complex joins easier to reason about.

slides.title: Protect target grain
slides.transcript:
A join can use a technically valid key and still be wrong for the analytical grain.

[tts-break]

Suppose the target result should contain one row per admission. We have already joined patients to admissions correctly. Now imagine adding lab results using patient ID only.

[tts-break]

If one patient has several admissions and several lab tests, each admission can pair with every lab result for that patient. The admission grain is no longer protected. A lab test that actually belongs to one encounter may appear beside another admission for the same patient.

[tts-break]

The deeper question is what the lab record belongs to. Does it belong to the patient generally, to a particular admission, or to a specific encounter? The database design should answer that. If the true relationship uses an encounter ID, joining only on patient ID is too broad.

[tts-break]

This mistake happens in many domains. A customer ID may exist in orders, payments, and support tickets, but that does not mean every payment belongs to every order. Always ask whether the key you are using matches the level of the relationship you need.

slides.title: Guided practice 1
slides.transcript:
This guided practice builds a department-level report.

[tts-break]

The requirement says every department must appear, including departments with zero activity. That tells us to start from departments and preserve that table. Admissions and medical staff are optional related data, so we LEFT JOIN them.

[tts-break]

A department can have several admissions and several staff members. Because both are one-to-many relationships, the joined detail rows can multiply. That is why the query uses COUNT DISTINCT for admission IDs, patient IDs, and staff IDs.

[tts-break]

The query also calculates average stay length and combines staff specializations into a readable list. After grouping, the final grain is one row per department.

[tts-break]

Run the query and find the department with no activity. It should still appear because departments is the preserved population. Then inspect a busy department and compare its counts with the underlying data.

[tts-break]

This structure is common in management dashboards where every region, program, department, or product category must remain visible even when activity is zero.

slides.title: Guided practice 2
slides.transcript:
This guided practice is a debugging exercise.

[tts-break]

The query joins patients to admissions, lab results, and prescriptions. Then it reports three different numbers: the total number of joined rows, a naive admission count, and a distinct admission count.

[tts-break]

The naive admission count uses COUNT on the admission ID without DISTINCT. Because an admission row can be repeated across combinations with several lab and prescription rows, that count may be larger than the true number of admissions.

[tts-break]

The distinct count uses the admission ID as the event key and removes repeated appearances of the same admission inside the joined result. Compare the two values carefully.

[tts-break]

The important question is not simply which number is smaller. Explain why the naive count can be inflated even though no admission was duplicated in the original admissions table. The duplication is created by the join combinations.

[tts-break]

This is the kind of debugging you will do in real analytical work. When a metric looks too large, inspect the relationship structure before assuming the source data is wrong.

slides.title: Guided practice 3
slides.transcript:
This practice asks you to predict the population before running the query.

[tts-break]

Choice A places the Glucose condition inside ON. Because patients is on the left side of the LEFT JOIN, every patient remains. The condition only controls which lab rows are eligible to match.

[tts-break]

Choice B places the Glucose condition in WHERE. The LEFT JOIN may initially preserve every patient, but the final WHERE filter removes rows where the lab test is not Glucose, including the NULL lab values for patients with no Glucose match.

[tts-break]

Before you press Run, state your prediction. Choice A should return every patient. Some rows will contain Glucose information and some will contain NULL lab values.

[tts-break]

Then run Choice A and verify the result. The point of this exercise is to build a habit of predicting semantics before execution. SQL becomes much easier to debug when you already know what kind of population and grain you expect.

slides.title: Project timeline
slides.transcript:
This is an optional integration project that combines JOIN thinking with a technique from earlier SQL work.

[tts-break]

The common table expression creates a patient timeline by stacking admissions, lab tests, and prescriptions with UNION ALL. Each source is transformed into the same basic shape: patient ID, event date, event type, and event details.

[tts-break]

At that stage, the grain is one event. Then we join the event stream to patients using patient ID so each event can include the patient's name. The join enriches the event rows without changing the event grain.

[tts-break]

This pattern is useful in many real projects. A customer journey could combine orders, website visits, support calls, and returns. A student timeline could combine registrations, submissions, advising appointments, and logins.

[tts-break]

Run the query and follow one patient across several dates. The main Module 6 lesson is to notice how clearly defining the event grain before the join makes the final result easier to understand and validate.

slides.title: Project transitions
slides.transcript:
This slide is an optional preview of a later SQL topic. The function LEAD is a window function, and window functions are covered later in the course. You do not need to memorize LEAD here.

[tts-break]

The reason this example appears in Module 6 is that the same grain reasoning still matters. Inside the common table expression, one row represents one admission, along with information about the next admission for the same patient.

[tts-break]

LEAD looks forward within each patient's admissions ordered by date. It retrieves the next department and the next admission date. The outer query keeps cases where a later admission exists and the department changes. Then it groups those transitions.

[tts-break]

In the current practice data, one example of a department change is a patient moving from Endocrinology to Cardiology on a later admission. After grouping, one row represents one transition pattern, such as one department to another department.

[tts-break]

Again, the important point for this module is not the window-function syntax. The important point is to keep asking what one row represents after each transformation. We will study window functions in more detail later.

slides.title: Assessment concepts
slides.transcript:
Before starting the coding exercises, make sure you can explain the main concepts in your own words.

[tts-break]

First, explain why a LEFT JOIN followed by a WHERE condition on the right table can remove unmatched left rows. A strong explanation should mention that unmatched right-side values become NULL and WHERE filters the final result.

[tts-break]

Second, choose a join from a population rule. Only matched records suggests INNER JOIN. Every patient suggests preserving patients with LEFT JOIN when patients is on the left. Reconciliation across both sources suggests FULL OUTER JOIN.

[tts-break]

Third, explain row multiplication without simply calling the extra rows duplicates. Several child tables can contain multiple matches, creating combinations of valid detail rows. Those combinations can inflate counts.

[tts-break]

Finally, explain how to produce one row per patient safely when several child tables contain activity. One strong strategy is to summarize each child table to patient grain before joining the summaries.

[tts-break]

If you can explain these ideas clearly, the syntax becomes easier to reconstruct when you need it.

slides.title: Assessment coding strategy
slides.transcript:
This slide summarizes the strategy behind the more advanced coding exercises.

[tts-break]

The target is one row per patient with three measures: admission count, lab count, and prescription count. Patients with no activity must still remain.

[tts-break]

The safest approach is to summarize each child table by patient ID first. After aggregation, each child summary contains at most one row per patient. Then we LEFT JOIN those summaries to the patient master.

[tts-break]

Because patients is preserved, a patient with no admissions, labs, or prescriptions still appears. COALESCE converts a missing count from NULL to zero, which is usually easier to interpret in a report.

[tts-break]

This is a common production pattern. A customer dashboard may combine order count, support-ticket count, and refund count. A student dashboard may combine registration count, advising visits, and submissions. Pre-aggregating each activity source protects the target grain.

[tts-break]

When you run the query, validate at least one patient with multiple activities and one patient with no activity. The output row count should equal the number of patients.

slides.title: Exercise 1 INNER JOIN
slides.transcript:
This is Coding Exercise 1. Your task is to return patient ID, patient name, admission ID, diagnosis, and department for patients who have admissions.

[tts-break]

The phrase patients who have admissions tells you that a match is required. We are not trying to preserve patients with no admission. That points toward INNER JOIN.

[tts-break]

Start with patients as one table and admissions as the related table. The relationship is patient ID. Select the requested columns and sort the result as instructed.

[tts-break]

Do not try to force one row per patient. The correct grain is one row per matching admission. If a patient has multiple admissions, that patient's information should appear on multiple rows.

[tts-break]

Before using Run and Check, predict what should happen to a patient with no admission. After running, compare the number of result rows with the number of matching admissions. If the checker does not pass, inspect the requested columns, join condition, and grain before changing syntax randomly.

slides.title: Exercise 2 LEFT JOIN
slides.transcript:
Coding Exercise 2 changes the population rule. This time, every patient must appear, even when the patient has no admission.

[tts-break]

The phrase every patient tells you which table must be preserved. Patients should be on the left side of a LEFT JOIN, while admissions is optional.

[tts-break]

Before running the query, predict what an unmatched patient should look like. The patient ID and name should still have values, while admission ID and diagnosis should be NULL.

[tts-break]

Also remember that LEFT JOIN does not automatically create one row per patient. A patient with several admissions can still appear several times. Preservation and grain are different concepts.

[tts-break]

Use Run and Check after you have written the join. If the unmatched patient disappears, examine whether you accidentally used INNER JOIN or added a filter that removes NULL admission rows.

slides.title: Exercise 3 Anti-join
slides.transcript:
Coding Exercise 3 asks you to return patients who do not have any lab results.

[tts-break]

Start by preserving all patients with a LEFT JOIN to lab results. When a patient has no matching lab row, the lab-side columns become NULL.

[tts-break]

Then choose a right-side key that cannot be NULL in a real matched record. The lab test ID is a good choice because it identifies the lab row. Keep only rows where that key is NULL.

[tts-break]

Read your logic as a sentence: keep all patients, try to match a lab result, and then keep only the patients for whom no lab row was found.

[tts-break]

This is the anti-join pattern. You can reuse the same reasoning to find customers with no orders, students with no submissions, employees with no training record, or products with no sales.

slides.title: Exercise 4 ON vs WHERE
slides.transcript:
Coding Exercise 4 checks whether you understand the difference between matching and final filtering.

[tts-break]

The requirement says every patient must remain, while only Glucose lab rows should be allowed to match. The words every patient are the key to the problem.

[tts-break]

Complete the ON clause by adding the Glucose condition to the matching rule. Do not move that condition into WHERE. If it goes into WHERE, patients without a Glucose match can disappear.

[tts-break]

Before running the query, predict the output. Every patient should appear. Some patients will have a Glucose test ID and result value. Other patients will have NULL lab fields.

[tts-break]

After Run and Check, inspect both types of rows. The goal is not only to pass the checker. The goal is to build the habit of deciding whether each condition belongs to matching or to final result filtering.

slides.title: Exercise 5 Safe counts
slides.transcript:
Coding Exercise 5 is the main cardinality exercise in the assignment.

[tts-break]

The required grain is one row per patient. You need an admission count, a lab count, and a prescription count, and patients with zero activity must still remain.

[tts-break]

Do not directly join all three detail tables and then count rows. That can create combinations and inflate the measures.

[tts-break]

Instead, summarize each child table by patient ID inside the provided common table expressions. Each summary should return one row per patient with one count. Then LEFT JOIN those summaries to patients.

[tts-break]

Use COALESCE so that a patient with no related activity shows zero instead of NULL.

[tts-break]

After Run and Check, validate the result. The number of output rows should equal the number of patients. Check a patient with several activities and a patient with no activity. This pattern is widely used when building dashboards and analytical feature tables.

slides.title: Exercise 6 Department metrics
slides.transcript:
The final coding exercise combines preservation, cardinality, and aggregation.

[tts-break]

The final result must contain one row per department, including departments with zero activity. That tells you to start from departments because departments is the population to preserve.

[tts-break]

LEFT JOIN admissions by department and LEFT JOIN medical staff by department. Because one department can have several admissions and several staff members, the combined rows can multiply.

[tts-break]

If you count every joined row directly, the measures can be inflated. Count distinct admission IDs for admission count and distinct staff IDs for staff count.

[tts-break]

Then GROUP BY department so the final grain is one row per department.

[tts-break]

After Run and Check, find the department with no activity. It should still appear with zero counts. Then inspect a busy department and make sure the values represent real admissions and real staff rather than multiplied join combinations.

slides.title: Complete Module
slides.transcript:
This is the completion page for Module 6 and Assignment 5.

[tts-break]

The module tracks ten knowledge checks and six coding exercises. Before selecting Complete Module, review the counters and make sure they reflect the work you intended to complete.

[tts-break]

If an activity is incomplete, the page lists it and lets you return to the relevant slide. When you select Complete Module, the page creates a Canvas submission summary containing your completion status, knowledge-check answers, and the SQL saved for each coding exercise.

[tts-break]

Review the generated Assignment 5 summary before copying it into Canvas. If your work is incomplete, the page will warn you, but it can still include the answers and SQL you have completed so far.

[tts-break]

Remember that progress is stored locally in the current browser. Switching devices, using a private browsing window, or clearing browser storage may remove that saved progress.

[tts-break]

Treat this final page as quality control. In professional data work, checking the output before submitting or publishing is just as important as writing the query.

slides.title: Summary
slides.transcript:
Let us summarize the main ideas from Module 6.

[tts-break]

Start with grain. Decide what one result row should represent before writing the join. Then decide what population must be preserved.

[tts-break]

INNER JOIN keeps only matches. LEFT JOIN and RIGHT JOIN preserve one designated side. FULL OUTER JOIN preserves unmatched rows from both sides.

[tts-break]

Remember that ON controls matching, while WHERE filters the joined result. This distinction becomes especially important with outer joins.

[tts-break]

Cardinality explains why rows repeat or multiply. One-to-many repetition can be completely correct, but several one-to-many child tables joined together can create combinations that inflate counts.

[tts-break]

When your target is one row per patient, customer, student, or department, pre-aggregating child tables to the target grain is often the clearest solution.

[tts-break]

Finally, validate. Compare total rows, distinct keys, unmatched cases, and known examples. If you keep one habit from this module, use this sequence: define the grain, predict the matches, run the join, and verify the result before trusting it.

slides.title: Next: Subqueries
slides.transcript:
The next module moves from joins to subqueries.

[tts-break]

A join combines row sets directly. A subquery allows one query to use the result of another query as part of its logic. You will use subqueries for questions involving membership, existence, comparisons, and supporting calculations.

[tts-break]

For example, you may ask which patients have a value above an overall average, which customers have at least one qualifying order, or which products have never appeared in a sales table.

[tts-break]

The join skills from this module still matter. When deciding between a join, a subquery, or a common table expression, continue asking about grain, cardinality, preservation, and clarity.

[tts-break]

Before moving on, make sure you can explain the difference between matching and preservation and why several detail tables can multiply rows. Those ideas will continue to appear in more advanced SQL.

[tts-break]

As SQL becomes more expressive, the goal is not to use the most advanced syntax. The goal is to write logic that is correct, understandable, and easy to validate.
